The complainant, Mert Aydın, reported that when he returned home in the evening his laptop, his wristwatch and the cash he kept in a drawer were missing. He states that he locked the door when he left in the morning. The initial inspection found no sign of forced entry on the front door; how the flat was entered could not be determined. The flowerpot beside the door was checked; no key was found in it. The laptop invoice Mert provided records the serial number as LQ7B-024861. When and by whom the missing items were taken has not yet been determined. Interviews with the people in the building and a review of the entrance record were deemed appropriate.

The complainant, Mert Aydın, reports that he left home in the morning and, on his return in the evening, could not find some of his belongings. He says he locked the door. The interview can draw out details about the house keys and his movements that day.
First interview record of Elif Demir, Mert Aydın’s former partner. She can be asked about their relationship, the belongings left at the flat and the day of the incident.
First interview record of Hasan Kaya, Mert Aydın’s neighbour across the landing. In his own words he describes what he saw in the building and his past contact with Mert.

Camera 01 records the building’s shared entrance. The log below lists the passages seen and the signal status. Who entered or left during an interval with no recording cannot be determined from this camera.

Elif Demir can be interviewed again about the building entrance record obtained after the first interview. Which line of the record was shown and the answer given are entered in the interview transcript.

The serial number LQ7B-024861 on the invoice submitted with the complaint matches the number of a device handed in at 14.10 on the day of the incident to a second-hand electronics shop in Beşiktaş. The shop’s receipt was issued in the name of Hasan Kaya.

An inspection can be requested to verify the device and the receipt.

SUBJECT OF INSPECTION — The laptop Mert Aydın reported missing.

The serial number on the invoice submitted with the complaint is LQ7B-024861. The intake records of the second-hand electronics shop in Beşiktaş for the day of the incident were searched. The serial number on the device left at the shop at 14.10 matches the invoice. The receipt was issued in the name of Hasan Kaya; a copy has been added to the file. The device has been secured.

This report documents that the device found matches the invoice and that the shop kept an intake record in the name of Hasan Kaya. It does not directly show how the device was taken out of Mert’s flat. There are no new findings about the missing wristwatch and cash.
Hasan Kaya can be interviewed again about the earlier statements and the new records. His answers are recorded separately for each source shown to him.

The device receipt issued in Hasan’s name matches the serial number of the missing laptop. The follow-up statement gives information about how the key was used. Elif’s lie revealed a visit she had hidden; it did not prove she committed the theft.

A statement is not evidence. Nor is a lie proof of guilt.
Elif’s first statement conflicts with the camera record. But that conflict does not show she stole the belongings. Reconsider the laptop’s serial number and the receipt issued in Hasan’s name.

Neighbour · Lives in the flat across the landing
When did you leave home, and when did you get back?

I left around half past eight in the morning; when I got back from work and opened the door it was getting dark. At first I thought everything was where it should be. When the laptop wasn’t on the desk, I checked for my watch, then the drawer.
Who else had a key to the flat?
I had my key with me. Elif had one too; I never took it back after we split up. I don’t remember giving a key to anyone else.
Is there a neighbour who might have seen something?
Hasan lives across the landing. I don’t know whether he was in the building during the day; but if he saw anything at the entrance, he could tell you.
What is your relationship with Mert?
We broke up a few days ago. Some of my things were still at his place; we hadn’t even discussed when I’d collect them. We don’t really see each other these days.
Did you go to Mert’s flat that day?
No. I didn’t go to Mert’s flat that day.
Who did you see in the building that day?
Around midday a woman was leaving the building. I saw her from the top of the stairs; we didn’t stop to talk.
Is there a record that could confirm that?
There’s a camera at the front door. I didn’t check the time; if you want to confirm who came through, there may be a record there.
Did you go into Mert’s flat that day?
No. I didn’t go into Mert’s flat that day.
Where were you around midday that day?
Her shoulders dropped. She took her hand off the table and clasped it in her lap.
Yes, I went into the building. I took the rest of my things without telling Mert. On my way out I left the key to the flat in the flowerpot by the door.
Why didn’t you say this in the first interview?
I went into his flat without telling him. When I heard about the burglary I thought that if I said so, everyone would look at me. So I lied; I’m not the one who stole his things.
Did you use to keep the spare key in the flowerpot?

I used to keep my own spare key in the flowerpot sometimes. Last month I got locked out; Hasan helped me. I took the key out of the flowerpot in front of him. Later I took that key back; the copy Elif had was a separate one. I can’t say whether Hasan knew he’d find a key in the flowerpot that day.
Did you know where Mert kept his spare key?
Mert got locked out once and I helped him. I didn’t notice where he took the key from. And how do you get from that to there being a key there that day?
Where were you around one in the afternoon?
Hands on the table, palms open. He answered without moving.
I was at home. Alone; I can’t point to anyone who could confirm it. The camera not working has nothing to do with me.

Are you sure you locked the door when you left?
I remember turning the key as I pulled the door shut. In the evening the door was as it should be; I didn’t see any break or scratch. Maybe it doesn’t matter, but the silence inside felt strange.
Did you speak to Mert that day?
No, I didn’t. After the break-up our conversations never ended easily; I didn’t want to call him.
Around what time did you see that woman?
It was close to lunchtime. I wasn’t looking at my phone; if I gave you an exact time I’d be making it up.
Which of your things did you take from the flat?
I took my clothes and my books. I remember the laptop being on the desk, but I can’t give an exact time for how long I stayed in the room. I didn’t touch his watch or his money.
How close are you to Hasan?
Hasan and I aren’t close beyond being neighbours. He helped me last month when I was locked out; other than that we hardly talk.
Did any of the missing items come into your hands?
He picked up the receipt, straightened its edge and put it back down. His voice did not change at all.
I took the laptop to the shop; the name on the receipt is mine. I won’t explain here how the device came to me. The receipt only shows the hand-over; I don’t accept that I went into Mert’s flat.

After a few years on patrol, Bora moved to the bube Department's investigation unit. The first files were closed in Istanbul; now the unit sends Bora country by country to the cases local teams could not solve. Calm and observant, Bora never tells anyone "you're lying" but sets what they said beside the records, and writes a conclusion only when the evidence can justify it.

She nodded when she heard the time. Her eyes stayed on the screen; her voice was flat.
Yes, the one who entered the building at 11.48 was me. I took a few of my things without telling Mert. On my way out I left the key of his I still had in the flowerpot beside his door.
She spoke quickly, as if she had put the sentence together beforehand. At the end she took a deep breath.
Yes, the one who left at 12.16 was me too. I had my own clothes and books with me. I didn’t take Mert’s key; I left it in the flowerpot beside his door.

Can you describe the day you ran into Mert at his door?
He leaned slightly forward as he spoke. After the sentence he kept his eyes on you.

All right. I was standing by the door; Mert bent down and fiddled with the flowerpot, so if he took the key from there I’d have seen it. But something I saw a month ago doesn’t show that I went into his flat that day.
How did you notice the items were missing?

The laptop is normally on the desk; it wasn’t there. I keep my wristwatch in the drawer; the money was in the same drawer. At first I thought I might have moved them myself, then I realised all three were gone at once. I also handed over the laptop’s invoice for the inspection.
Why didn’t you take Elif’s key back?
We were going to talk about a day for her to collect her things, but we never set a date. I kept putting off asking for the key too. After the break-up I didn’t want to reopen things between us.
Were any of your things still at Mert’s flat?
A few clothes, two or three books. I didn’t want to argue again over them. Mert and I hadn’t agreed when I’d collect them.
Why didn’t you speak to Mert at all that day?
Every conversation came back to the break-up. Please don’t take that as a sign of anything else; I told you I didn’t go to the flat.
How did you recognise the woman you saw?
I’d seen her with Mert a few times. I didn’t know her name. I thought the woman leaving through the building door looked like her; I only saw her face briefly.
How much did you see of Mert before?
We’re neighbours; we say hello when we run into each other. He was locked out once; I stood with him and helped. Then everyone went back to their own flat.
Why didn’t you hand the key to Mert in person?
I didn’t want to keep the key any more, and I didn’t want to face him either. The flowerpot was where Mert used to keep a spare key. I don’t know who looked there after me.
Did you call Mert when you heard about the burglary?
I didn’t. I thought that if I kept quiet I’d stay out of it; now I see I did the opposite.
Who else might have known where the key in the flowerpot was?
Elif knew; I’d told her in the past. Hasan also saw me take the key from the flowerpot the day I was locked out. I don’t know who else saw.

She twisted the hair tie on her wrist as she spoke. Her voice rose mid-sentence.
She was silent for a while. Then she looked straight at you and did not look away.
I didn’t give the key back. I didn’t want to, either. I know saying that counts against me; even so, I didn’t open that door.
She leaned over the paper and read the line twice. Her hands were trembling.
If the neighbour saw me, he didn’t see wrong. That week I went to that building, up to the door. I didn’t ring the bell; I turned back. You don’t have to believe me.
He didn’t even look at the screen. He repeated himself in the same flat tone.
He rubbed the edge of the table with his thumb. His voice slowed.
He put a hand to the back of his neck, then lowered it. His voice was flat.
A short, hard laugh. She pushed the chair back but did not stand up.
He says “close to lunchtime”. I was there close to lunchtime too. I didn’t keep track of the time; if I had, would I be more believable?
Her face reddened. She said the end of the sentence as if swallowing it.
He may not know me, but the person he describes looks like me. I’m saying that myself, before you ask.
She lowered her gaze to the table. She spoke after a long silence.
We were going to talk about my things; we never managed to. That’s why I was there that day too, to talk. Nobody opened the door.
She leaned back in the chair. For the first time she spoke without hurrying.
I knew about the flowerpot. I lived in that flat for a year; it would be strange if I didn’t. Someone who knew is sitting in front of you, that’s the point.
He watched the frames closely, then shrugged.
He read the report at length. His voice grew a little hoarse as he answered.
A tired smile. He sprawled in his seat.
He folded his arms, then unfolded them. His gaze stayed on the table.
He said the same sentence with the same emphasis for the third time.
She’s the one who went in. I didn’t even step out of my door that day. If you want me to say it again, I will.
When he mentioned the cupboard he waved a hand towards the door. He looked at ease.
He took the key from the flowerpot, fine. I’ve got neither a key nor any of his things. Let me make it easy: there’s a box in the cupboard, full of books.
As he described the landing he traced a circle on the table with his finger.
There are ten flats in this building. Most of them live alone like me, and all their doors open onto the same landing.
He said it without blinking. Then he looked at the window.
We’re not close. We didn’t talk long at the door either. If we did talk, I don’t remember.
Half a smile. His hands stayed still on the table.
Knowing is one thing, going in is another. But being on the list of people who knew puts you in this chair, I’ve learned that much.
He turned the screen slightly towards himself with his hand. He looked at it for a long time.
She’s in the record. You’re asking me about the day at the door. If there’s something connecting the two, it isn’t with me.
His voice dropped as he talked about money trouble. He didn’t finish.
I know that shop; I’ve done business there before. That isn’t what we talked about at the door; he mentioned money trouble, that’s all.
He paused for a moment when he heard the date. Then he spoke clearly.
He stopped mid-sentence and started again.
He asked you to show the frames again. The second time he said the same thing.
She was carrying something; I couldn’t see what. It would be easy to pin something I couldn’t see on me, I realise that.
A short silence. Then he shrugged and answered.
We’re not close. If we were, maybe he’d have left something with me, and then I’d have something in my hands. As it is, I don’t.
He leaned forward and spoke, separating the words.
You’re mixing up the key and the belongings. If ten people knew where it was, the one who took them could be any of them. It isn’t me.
He hesitated. The end of the sentence came out like a question.
He thought I might have seen something. Even if I did, I can’t say for sure whether I was in the building that day. I’ve been mixing up days lately.
He didn’t look at the record. The answer was ready.
You’re showing me her leaving and asking me about the day at the door. We’re talking about the same person, but not the same day.
I don’t know what you expect me to say when you show me this. I’ve told you what I know.
If you’re drawing a link between this and me, you say what it is. I can’t see it.
I don’t see what this has to do with me. If you have something else to ask, ask.

Don’t rush. Before a file closes, you can rethink the same question against different records.
Statement: information a person gives in their own words. Until evidence supports it, it is only a claim.
Evidence: a concrete record or object showing that something happened. When it contradicts a statement, evidence carries the weight.
Presumption of innocence: everyone is innocent until proven guilty. Suspicion alone is not a conclusion.
Benefit of the doubt: if the evidence does not clearly prove a conclusion, the decision does not go against the accused.
Timeline: putting events in order by time makes the gaps between statements visible.
Eyewitness: someone who saw the event themselves. A hearsay witness repeats what they heard from others.
Cross-examination: testing a statement against another record. You can present a record only if the person is named in it.
Chain of custody: the record of who held a piece of evidence from the moment it was found until it entered the file.
Reasoned conclusion: a report must answer not only 'who' but also 'based on which evidence'.
A false accusation costs more than an incomplete report. If you are unsure, widen the evidence.
Alibi: a claim that the person was somewhere else at the time. Until verified, it is a statement.
Minutes: the official written record of an interview or procedure. What was said can be compared with what was written.
Camera records do not show everything: blind spots and signal gaps are information too.
Scene: the place where the crime happened or its traces were found. Locations in records are read against it.

The assignment at the Germany branch has been completed successfully. The Arendt ledger has been accepted as evidence, and files closed in London and Berlin have been reopened. As the ledger’s final recipient is in Tokyo, the assignment has been transferred to the bube Tokyo branch.
— The review of the Kisaragi file is complete.
— There’s an auction in Paris. In the catalogue, a bowl from Kamakura.

The assignment at the Japan branch has been completed successfully. Kisaragi Shōji’s role in the Arendt ledger has been documented as that of an intermediary, and files closed in Tokyo have been reassessed. As the trail of goods and transfers extends to Paris, the assignment has been passed to the bube Paris — Belleville branch.
— The review of the Delorme file is complete.
— There’s a warehouse in Chicago, in Pilsen. Lakeshore is written on its door.

The assignment at the France branch has been completed successfully. The role of Maison Delorme’s shipping department in the Arendt ledger has been documented; the Lot 47, Fontainebleau and Le Marais files have been linked to the same chain. As the Lakeshore Freight manifests and the provenance letters signed by Dr. E. Varga extend to Chicago, the assignment has been passed to the bube Chicago — Pilsen branch.
— The review of the Lakeshore file is complete.
— In Naples, at the port, there’s a family firm. A name comes up in a voice recording: Edda.

The assignment at the USA branch has been completed successfully. Lakeshore Freight’s role in the Arendt ledger has been documented as shipping and money-laundering intermediary; the Pilsen, Bridgeport, Loop and Gold Coast files have been linked to the same chain. As the payments and shipments extend to the port of Naples, the assignment has been passed to the bube Naples — Quartieri Spagnoli branch.
— The review of the Caruso file is complete.
— There’s a foundation in Seville. A consultant’s name is on the trustee list. And a Spanish number that doesn’t answer.

The assignment at the Italy branch has been completed successfully. Caruso Marittima’s role in the Arendt ledger has been documented as port, shipping and forged-document intermediary; the Quartieri Spagnoli, Forcella, Montesanto, San Gregorio Armeno, Procida and port files have been linked to the same chain. As the messages and shipments extend to Spain, the assignment has been passed to the bube Seville — Triana branch.
— The review of the Santa Ana file is complete.
— There’s a reinsurance company in Montreal. The beneficiary’s name is very like ours. You noticed that too, didn’t you?

The assignment at the Spain branch has been completed successfully. Fundación Santa Ana’s donation, sale and consultancy payments since 1989 have been documented through the Triana, Guadalquivir, cooperative and archive files; the registered consultant has been identified as Dr. Edda Varga. As the payments extend to Montreal, the assignment has been passed to the bube Montreal — Mile End branch.
— The review of the Laurentide file is complete.
— For the first time, an answer came from Melbourne. One word. The Footscray branch is expecting you.

The assignment at the Canada branch has been completed successfully. The policies of Laurentide Réassurance’s ‘special programmes’ arm in the Mile End, Aréna du Parc, Entrepôt des Érablières, Le Sous-Sol, Rue Waverly and Silo Lemoyne files have been documented; the beneficiary of the claim payments has been identified as the ‘bube International Liaison Programme’, its director Edda Varga. As the last transfer extends to Australia, the assignment has been passed to the bube Melbourne — Footscray branch.
(You pick up the receiver. The line is open; there is no one on the other end.)
— The review of the Liaison file is complete.
(A long silence. Then the line goes dead.)
(On the desk lies an empty envelope with a Budapest postmark. Sender: E. V.)

The assignment at the Australia branch has been completed successfully. Pacific Liaison Trust’s role in the Footscray fish market, Flemington stables, Maribyrnong marina, tram tender, Williamstown port and Hopkins Street files has been documented; the 1989 founding file of the ‘International Liaison Programme’ has been shared with the branches of nine countries. The whereabouts of director Dr. Edda Varga could not be established. The file remains open.
